question: After Rome, which fats survive where — and what do cooks, monks, stewards and herders keep going?
thesis: After Rome the map of fat splits in three. The Latin north runs on butter, tallow, pork and whale, with monasteries and the church keeping a thin line of oil alive; the Islamic world cooks in tail fat and sesame and olive oil and thinks of fat in terms of the humours; and in Asia the Tang court eats dairy fat, Japan bans meat and cooks without oil, and South India presses sesame and burns ghee in temple lamps.

big_ideas.title: The Latin north lives on butter, pork and whale
big_ideas.text: Butter in Anglo-Saxon England is a luxury, a by-product of ewes’ milk cheese; Irish butter is buried in bogs; Frankish stewards must account for fat, tallow and soap; and pigs are fed on the autumn mast. Beyond the farm the sea gives fat: Norwegians hunt whales and walrus, and Icelandic families fight over a stranded whale.

big_ideas.title: Oil survives in a few places
big_ideas.text: Monasteries and cathedrals keep olive-oil expertise alive for holy oils and lamps, the Prophet is said to anoint himself with olive oil, Spanish takes its oil words from Arabic, and Italy turns soap into a craft. Sesame is named as a crop of Iran.

big_ideas.title: Baghdad cooks with fat and judges it as medicine
big_ideas.text: The tenth-century cookbook fries meat in sheep’s tail fat, rubs bread with sesame or unripe-olive oil and judges each fat by its effect on the humours: butter ‘floats’ at the stomach’s mouth, but clarified butter is better.

big_ideas.title: Asia’s tables and lamps: dairy and ghee, oil and abstinence
big_ideas.text: The part-Turkic Tang court is the climax of Chinese dairy fat, with kaymak and ti-hu at banquets, while its monasteries burn oil in an ever-burning lamp. South India presses sesame and endows temple lamps with flocks of sheep for ghee. Japan goes the other way: it bans meat in 675 and cooks without oil.

threads.title: Butter, pork and whale in the Latin north
threads.claim: The fats of the north are animal and dairy, and the sea is part of the larder.

beats.text: Butter in Anglo-Saxon England comes from ewes’ milk and is a lord’s luxury.
Pigs are pastured in the forest on the autumn mast, and mast rights outweigh timber as forest income.
The Capitulary De Villis tells royal stewards to account for fat, tallow, butter and soap.
Irish butter is buried in the peat in wooden firkins and bladders.
Ohthere describes hunting whales and walrus on the White Sea; whaling is certain in the North Sea by the 800s.
In the Icelandic sagas families fight over the ownership of whale carcasses.

threads.title: Where oil and plant fat survive
threads.claim: In a world of butter and lard, oil and tree fats are held by the church, by Islam, by Italian craftsmen and by African farmers.

beats.text: Monasteries and cathedrals remain islands of oil expertise for holy oils and church lamps.
In tradition the Prophet uses so much olive oil that his shawl is often drenched with it.
Spanish aceite and aceituna come from Andalusi Arabic az-zayt and az-zaytūna.
At Kirikongo in Burkina Faso, shea nuts leave a continuous record of use from about 100 to 1500 AD.
Soap is a craft by now, above all in Italy, made from tallow in the north and olive oil in the south.
Abu Mansur names sesame as a crop of Iran.

threads.title: Baghdad’s kitchen and body
threads.claim: A single tenth-century cookbook shows the fats of an Islamic city and the reasons given for them.

beats.text: Meat is first fried in rendered sheep’s tail fat, ‘sweated’ to remove bad odours.
Bread is rubbed with sesame oil or the oil of unripe olives before it meets the oven wall.
Fats are weighed by their effect on the humours: butter floats at the stomach’s mouth, clarified butter does not.

threads.title: Tang China: dairy fat, lamps and seed oil
threads.claim: The Tang court makes dairy fat a status food, and its farmers and monasteries make oil a routine.

beats.text: Cream, yogurt, cheese and butter are popular, a climax of Chinese dairy fat.
Pharmacologists argue whether cow or goat kaymak is better, and it goes into banquet pastries.
Iranian vendors sell ‘foreign’ cakes fried in fragrant oil on the street corners of the capital.
An oil lamp that is never allowed to go out is a symbol in Tang monasteries.
The Tang pharmacopoeia sets a ladder of milk, soured milk, su and ti hu as the stages of the soul.
A late-Tang farm calendar lists pressing seeds for oil among the tasks of the fourth month.

threads.title: Japan without oil, South India with it
threads.claim: Two Buddhist and Hindu worlds make opposite choices about fat.

beats.text: Tamil texts describe the sesame press, the chekku, and sesame oil is exported from the south.
Emperor Temmu bans eating beef, horse, dog, monkey and chicken in the farming months, on pain of execution.
Japan’s court makes so, a milk-skin product, and takes it as tribute and for medicine.
Cooking is done almost without oil or fat, and sesame oil is kept for the nobility’s fried cakes.
Chola temples are given flocks of 90 to 96 sheep to supply ghee for a perpetual lamp.

turning_points.text: The Tamil sesame press, the chekku, is in use.
The Prophet’s olive oil enters Islamic tradition.
Dairy fat reaches its peak at the Tang court.
The Tang pharmacopoeia fixes the Buddhist ladder from milk to ti hu.
Japan’s first ban on meat eating.
Spanish takes its oil words from Arabic.
Frankish stewards must account for fat, tallow and soap.
Pressing seeds is a farm task in Tang China.
Chola temples endow lamps with flocks of sheep.
The Baghdad cookbook puts tail fat and oil in the pot.

text: Nine entries, from the Frankish estates to the Irish bogs: the north’s fat is butter, tallow and soap, kept by stewards, hidden against raiders, fought over when a whale strands, and pork fat fed on the autumn mast of the forest ([[o1]], [[ec1]], [[ec2]], [[c1]], [[ec5]], [[ec10]]); the church and Arabic keep the Mediterranean’s oil in the picture ([[b1]], [[th1]], [[ec4]]).

Baghdad and the Prophet: cooking, dietetics and an oil anecdote ([[e1]], [[e2]], [[th2]], [[b4]]). The library holds the cookbook but not the Islamic agricultural writers. Abu Mansur names sesame as a crop of Iran in the late tenth century ([[ec11]]).

The densest non-European record: the Tamil press and the Chola lamp-endowments, the Tang calendar, the monastery lamp, the Buddhist ladder, Tang kaymak, ti-hu and fried foreign cakes, and Japan, which bans meat in 675, cooks without oil and takes a milk-skin tribute ([[ec3]], [[b5]], [[te1]], [[b2]], [[b3]], [[ec9]], [[e4]], [[o2]], [[e3]], [[ec6]], [[ec8]]).

One entry: the shea record at Kirikongo, Burkina Faso ([[ec7]]). Africa’s fat history in these centuries is far larger than one entry; the library holds no source on Ethiopia, the Sahel’s herders, the Maghreb’s oil or the Swahili coast.
No entry. The search found nothing in the library on Maya, Andean or Arctic fats in 600–1000.
No entry. Pacific coconut voyages are in an earlier folio, with a placeholder date.

sources.intro: A thin and uneven record: a translated Baghdad cookbook, a translated Frankish extract, South Indian inscriptions, a popular history of butter, Achaya, Needham, Anderson, Chang and Ishige for Asia, and Mueller, Ward and Ellis for Europe; three entries (Japan’s *so*, Spanish oil words, Kirikongo shea) rest on web summaries and one (the Prophet’s oil) on an unsourced anecdote.
main: Nasrallah’s translation of Ibn Sayyar for Baghdad ([[e1]], [[e2]], [[th2]]); the Fordham extract of the Capitulary De Villis ([[o1]]); South Indian Inscriptions vol. 23 ([[b5]]).

Needham and Kieschnick for the Tang entries ([[te1]], [[b2]], [[b3]]); Achaya for the Tamil press ([[ec3]]); Khosrova for butter ([[ec1]], [[ec2]]); Ward for soap ([[ec4]]); Ellis for whales ([[ec5]], [[c1]]).
Ishige for Japan ([[o2]], [[e3]]); Anderson and Chang (Schafer’s Tang chapter) for Tang dairy and the foreign cakes ([[ec8]], [[ec9]], [[e4]]).
Mortazavian, in Bedigian’s *Sesame* volume, for Abu Mansur ([[ec11]]).
contested: Mueller’s monastic ‘islands of oil’ cite no councils ([[b1]]); his anecdote of the Prophet’s oil names no source ([[b4]]).
The thousand-year-old Irish butter is a museum label as reported ([[ec2]]); the Icelandic sagas postdate the events ([[c1]]).
Spanish oil words show language, not the introduction of the crop ([[th1]]); the Kirikongo and *so* entries rest on abstracts and encyclopedia pages, not the papers ([[ec7]], [[ec6]]).
gaps: The Islamic agricultural writers are not covered: Watson’s *Agricultural Innovation in the Early Islamic World* (or an alternative) is not held, and Andalusian, Sicilian and Maghrebi (Ifriqiyan) olive oil are missing.

Africa has one entry; nothing on Aksum and Ethiopia’s butter and oilseeds, Nubia, the Sahel’s pastoral fats or the Swahili coast. Central Asia and the steppe, Tibet, Southeast Asia, the Americas (Maya, Andes) and the Pacific have no entry in these centuries; the search for them found no source in the library, and Reid’s book on Southeast Asia, now added, starts at 1450.

how_to_read: Read the thesis and the big ideas first, then the threads: each runs in date order and points to the entries that carry it. Entries that no thread needs are still reached through the regional picture and the lists.

Twenty-six entries, so read straight through. The *picture by region* counts the 26 entries: Europe 9, Near East 5, Far East 11, Africa 1; none in Americas, Oceania or Worldwide. Several dates are ranges for ‘the early Middle Ages’ because the sources do not narrow them. The Far East carries the folio, with Europe second and Africa a single entry.
The next folio is where documents (customs, Lent rules, Geniza ledgers, whale taxes) make fats countable.
